transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Deep dive: Dedicated staged rollouts (routing + control plane) walkthrough
Recorded: 2025-01-23 17:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Ethan Park, Mina Haddad, Jordan Lee, Chloe Martin, Logan Wright, Sean Gallagher
HelioBank: Priya Shah, Derek Lin, Ana Morales, Tom Becker, Speaker 6

Summary (auto-generated)
- Redwood walked through the Dedicated staged rollout architecture: control-plane RolloutPlan/Stage/Gate objects, routing enforcement of stage weights, and a server-side gate evaluator.
- HelioBank asked detailed questions on determinism (traffic stickiness, hashing inputs, what happens when capacity changes) and failure handling (missing metrics, evaluator lag, partial control-plane outages).
- Discussed safe defaults: hold on missing metrics, manual approvals between stages, audit log events for all operator actions, and capacity guardrails to avoid saturating reserved pools.

Topics
- Control plane: plan versioning, idempotency, and stage state machine
- Routing: deterministic allocation, 0%/100% transitions, and tenant isolation on reserved pools
- Gates: evaluation windows, metric freshness, and what “fail safe” means (pause/hold vs rollback)
- Failure modes: evaluator degraded, metrics late, routing policy mismatch, and how to prevent "split brain"
- Auditability: approvals and event trails for compliance

Questions captured (auto)
- What is the exact hash key for deterministic allocation (request id vs user id vs conversation id)?
- How do weight changes behave when the dedicated pool scales up/down (nodes added/removed)?
- If the gate evaluator is down, can traffic still shift? What does the system do by default?
- If metrics are missing or delayed, do you block advancement or auto-rollback?
- Can we require two-person approval for stage promotion and keep an auditable trail?

Transcript

[00:00] Ethan Park: Alright, we’ll get started. Thanks everyone. The goal today is a routing plus control plane walkthrough for the staged rollouts work for Dedicated pools. We’ll stay pretty technical.

[00:17] Priya Shah: Great. We’ve got Derek from SRE and Tom from security on. We’re trying to understand determinism and failure handling, like what happens when stuff goes sideways.

[00:28] Mina Haddad: Yep, that’s the right focus. A lot of this is about making sure we don’t accidentally blow up a reserved pool with a bad change.

[00:40] Chloe Martin: And also what you’ll see in the Console, but we can keep it mostly backend today unless you want screens.

[00:47] Ana Morales: Backend is fine. Screens later.

[00:55] Ethan Park: Cool. I’ll start with the control-plane primitives. Conceptually we have a RolloutPlan attached to a Dedicated pool. That plan has stages: Stage 0, Stage 1, Stage 2, etc. Each stage has an allocation weight and gates. Gates are conditions evaluated over a time window.

[01:18] Derek Lin: Allocation weight means percent of traffic to new model/runtime config, right?

[01:23] Mina Haddad: Right. It’s effectively two “targets”: baseline and candidate. In our implementation we call them current and next sometimes, but it’s a stage-based split.

[01:34] Jordan Lee: And important: it’s deterministic allocation, not random per-request. The same “key” should land in the same bucket consistently.

[01:44] Priya Shah: Let’s drill into that key. What do you hash on? Because if it’s request id, then it’s not stable.

[01:52] Jordan Lee: Exactly, so request id is not stable. The default for Dedicated is we look for an explicit routing key in the request context. In our API/SDK we can pass something like user_id or conversation_id. If none is provided, we fall back to a derived key that’s stable-ish per connection, but we strongly recommend setting it.

[02:12] Ana Morales: Derived key like IP? That’s dangerous for NAT.

[02:16] Jordan Lee: Not IP. More like a session token in the gateway layer. But yeah, it’s not ideal. So the guidance is: you provide a stable key.

[02:27] Mina Haddad: One thing we can do for beta is make it required for certain routes, but we’re balancing backwards compatibility.

[02:36] Tom Becker: For compliance, we also want predictability. Like if we’re doing a canary and we investigate a user complaint, we need to know if they were in canary.

[02:44] Jordan Lee: Yep. With deterministic allocation you can re-compute: given key K and stage weight W, you know if it landed in candidate. We also log the decision at the routing layer, sampled.

[03:00] Ethan Park: On the control plane side, the plan is versioned. Any update increments plan_version. Routing pulls policy snapshots. That matters for audit and for “what config was in effect at time T”.

[03:13] Derek Lin: If you change weight from 5 to 25 percent, is that a new stage or updating stage?

[03:18] Ethan Park: In our model, each stage has a configured weight, and stage progression is a transition. You can update the plan, but there are guardrails. Like you can’t jump from Stage 1 to Stage 3 without approvals if policy requires it.

[03:33] Chloe Martin: In the UI, it’ll look like “promote to next stage” rather than “edit weight on the fly,” for exactly that reason.

[03:41] Priya Shah: So what’s the actual state machine? Like, pending, running, paused, held…

[03:47] Ethan Park: Roughly: DRAFT -> ACTIVE. Within ACTIVE, a stage can be EVALUATING, WAITING_APPROVAL, PAUSED (hold), FAILED (if explicitly aborted/rolled back), or COMPLETED.

[04:03] Sean Gallagher: Operationally, we treat hold/pause as the safe state. If anything is ambiguous—missing metrics, evaluator behind—we stop advancing.

[04:14] Derek Lin: You said evaluator behind. So evaluator is separate from policy engine?

[04:19] Ethan Park: Correct. We decided to run gate evaluation server-side as an evaluator service. It queries metrics, computes gate status, writes results back to the control plane. Routing does not evaluate gates inline.

[04:35] Priya Shah: Why not inline? Wouldn’t that be simpler?

[04:38] Jordan Lee: Inline gate eval makes routing dependent on metrics queries. That’s high latency and failure-prone. Also cardinality issues. So we keep routing deterministic and fast.

[04:51] Logan Wright: And metrics pipelines aren’t instant. Some signals come in with a minute or two delay, depending on aggregation.

[05:01] Ana Morales: Ok. Then if evaluator is down, what happens? Does the rollout freeze?

[05:07] Sean Gallagher: Yes. Freeze/hold. The rollout won’t auto-advance. Traffic stays at the current stage weight.

[05:15] Priya Shah: Does it ever auto-roll back on evaluator failure?

[05:19] Sean Gallagher: Not by default. We don’t want an unrelated metrics outage to trigger a rollback that maybe causes more churn. So default is: hold.

[05:31] Tom Becker: But could you configure a hard fail, like if evaluator dead for 30 minutes, revert?

[05:36] Ethan Park: Not in v1, but we’ve discussed an “evaluator health gate” that can enforce conditions. For beta we’ll likely keep it conservative.

[05:49] Derek Lin: So what causes rollback automatically then?

[05:52] Sean Gallagher: Gate failures can be configured as hold or rollback. For Dedicated, recommended is hold-first. Then a human decides.

[06:02] Mina Haddad: Because rollback isn’t always safe either, if the candidate is the only one warm in cache, etc. But we can get into that.

[06:11] Priya Shah: Yeah please. For us, rollback is better than bad p95 for 40 minutes.

[06:17] Mina Haddad: Understood. The “hold vs rollback” is per gate policy. For example if 5xx rate spikes above threshold for N minutes, that might be auto-rollback. For latency creeping, we might hold.

[06:33] Logan Wright: Another nuance: “missing metrics” is treated separately. Missing metrics means “we don’t know,” so we pause. Not rollback.

[06:44] Ana Morales: What counts as missing? Like no datapoints?

[06:47] Logan Wright: Exactly. Or if the metrics lag exceeds a freshness bound. So if our metric timestamp is older than X, we treat as stale.

[07:02] Derek Lin: What’s X?

[07:04] Logan Wright: We’re currently proposing something like: require at least one datapoint per minute for key signals, and freshness less than 3 minutes. But it’s tunable.

[07:18] Priya Shah: Ok. Back to determinism. If the pool scales, does the traffic assignment change?

[07:25] Jordan Lee: Good question. Deterministic assignment to candidate vs baseline is independent of which node. That part is hash(K) < W. Then once it’s in candidate, there’s a second routing decision to pick a backend replica. That uses consistent hashing + load signals.

[07:43] Derek Lin: So if replicas change, a user might move between candidate replicas but still stay in candidate.

[07:48] Jordan Lee: Exactly.

[07:50] Ana Morales: And baseline/candidate is also pinned? Like sticky over time?

[07:55] Jordan Lee: Sticky as long as the stage weight and hash function remain the same, and you use the same key.

[08:03] Priya Shah: What if we change weight from 5% to 25%? Then some keys reclassify.

[08:08] Jordan Lee: Correct. That’s expected. It’s deterministic for a given weight. When you promote a stage, the cutoff changes.

[08:18] Tom Becker: Can we record which users were in which stage at time of an incident?

[08:23] Jordan Lee: We don’t store a user list. But we can log sampled routing decisions, and you can re-evaluate for a user if you know the key, stage weight, and plan_version.

[08:36] Ethan Park: That’s why plan_version is in audit and routing logs.

[08:43] Chloe Martin: And the Console will show “Plan v12 currently at Stage 2 (25%)” etc.

[08:52] Priya Shah: Let’s talk about partial failures. Suppose control plane is degraded. Can routing proceed?

[09:00] Ethan Park: Routing uses cached policy snapshots. If it can’t fetch updates, it continues using last known good. But it will not advance stage unless it receives an explicit updated snapshot.

[09:12] Derek Lin: So the “promote stage” is a control-plane write, evaluator sees it, then routing eventually picks it up.

[09:18] Ethan Park: Exactly.

[09:20] Derek Lin: What’s the propagation time?

[09:22] Mina Haddad: Typically seconds. But we design for minutes. And we’ll show “effective” vs “requested” in status.

[09:33] Ana Morales: That matters. If someone hits promote and thinks it’s live but it’s not, it’s confusing.

[09:38] Chloe Martin: Yep, we’ve got that feedback. The stage view will show: “Promotion requested at 17:23, routing applied at 17:24” type thing.

[09:49] Sean Gallagher: And if it’s not applied, we alert, because that can cause rollouts to get stuck.

[10:01] Priya Shah: How do you avoid split brain? Like two evaluators or two control-plane writers.

[10:07] Ethan Park: Single writer semantics via optimistic concurrency on plan_version, and evaluator uses leases. If it can’t renew lease, it stops writing results.

[10:19] Jordan Lee: Also stage transitions are idempotent. Promote stage includes an idempotency key. So retries don’t create multiple promotions.

[10:30] Derek Lin: Is that exposed to customer API?

[10:33] Ethan Park: For beta, probably operator-only, but the API design includes it.

[10:41] Tom Becker: On approvals: can we require two-person approvals? Like maker-checker.

[10:47] Ethan Park: The model supports approval policy per stage transition. For example: “requires role: DedicatedOperator” and “requires N approvals”. The audit trail includes approver identity.

[11:02] Chloe Martin: In UI, approvals is a modal listing required approvals and who already approved.

[11:08] Priya Shah: Ok. We want an audit export too.

[11:11] Tom Becker: Yeah, SOC-ish controls: who changed what when.

[11:16] Ethan Park: We emit audit events: rollout_plan.created, updated, stage.promoted, stage.approved, rollout.aborted, rollout.held.auto, things like that.

[11:31] Derek Lin: Let’s go to gates. What are the default gates?

[11:35] Sean Gallagher: For Dedicated: p95 latency, 5xx error rate, timeouts, queue depth, GPU utilization optionally. We don’t like GPU util as a hard gate alone, because it can be high but healthy.

[11:51] Logan Wright: Queue depth and timeouts are generally better “saturation” signals.

[11:56] Priya Shah: Our main pain is queuing. A bad model update can saturate reserved pool and queue grows. Can you gate on queue depth increase vs absolute threshold?

[12:08] Logan Wright: Yes, both. Absolute thresholds are simpler. Relative change is trickier but we can do it with baseline comparison.

[12:20] Jordan Lee: Just to be careful: comparing baseline vs candidate requires stable traffic and enough volume. At 5% you might not have enough.

[12:30] Ana Morales: That’s our question. At 5% traffic, quality of metrics is noisy.

[12:36] Logan Wright: Right. So default evaluation windows are longer at low traffic. Like Stage 1 might require 15 minutes, Stage 2 maybe 10, etc.

[12:49] Sean Gallagher: And there’s also a “minimum request count” gate. If you don’t have enough samples, you can’t advance.

[13:01] Priya Shah: That’s good. If we only have 100 rps, then 5% is 5 rps, maybe too low.

[13:07] Mina Haddad: Exactly. We can recommend stage weights based on volume.

[13:14] Speaker 6: Quick one on networking—does any of this require changes in our VPC peering? Sorry if off-topic.

[13:20] Mina Haddad: For Dedicated, no changes. Routing happens in our control plane + data plane side. If you’re private connectivity, it stays the same.

[13:32] Derek Lin: Back to failure. Suppose a gate fails due to real latency regression. What’s the immediate action? Does traffic go back to 0 for candidate?

[13:42] Sean Gallagher: If configured for auto-rollback, yes: stage transitions back to previous stable stage. If configured as hold, traffic stays at current weight but stops advancing.

[13:55] Priya Shah: But holding at 25% could still be painful.

[13:59] Sean Gallagher: Right, that’s why for high severity gates we recommend rollback. For example 5xx > 1% for 5 minutes might rollback.

[14:10] Tom Becker: Is rollback a separate plan version?

[14:13] Ethan Park: Yes, rollback is an event that changes effective stage. We record it in audit logs with reason: auto gate failure or manual abort.

[14:26] Ana Morales: Are you doing “abort” vs “rollback”? Like abort ends the rollout completely.

[14:31] Chloe Martin: In UI we use “Abort rollout” which effectively returns traffic to baseline and marks rollout as aborted. There’s also “Pause” which is hold.

[14:45] Priya Shah: How do you guarantee tenant isolation? Like if another tenant is rolling out, do we share evaluator resources?

[14:52] Ethan Park: Evaluator service is multi-tenant, but isolation is via per-tenant work queues and rate limits. The Dedicated pool itself is isolated GPU fleet, so traffic mixing does not happen.

[15:06] Logan Wright: On metrics, we make sure dimensions are low-cardinality: tenant_id, pool_id, route_id maybe, but not user_id.

[15:18] Derek Lin: Ok. What about capacity constraints during partial rollout? You might effectively run two model versions side by side and need more memory.

[15:28] Mina Haddad: Great point. On Dedicated reserved pools, we can’t conjure GPUs. So we have a guardrail: candidate must fit within headroom. If enabling candidate causes too much pressure (KV cache, weights memory), you either reduce concurrency or you can’t proceed.

[15:45] Jordan Lee: Routing also has a fallback policy: if candidate is overloaded, it can shed candidate traffic back to baseline. But that can violate strict stickiness. So it’s configurable.

[16:00] Priya Shah: Wait, shed candidate traffic back to baseline means a user flips.

[16:04] Jordan Lee: Yes. That’s why we treat it as a last resort safety valve to preserve availability. And we log when it happens.

[16:13] Ana Morales: That’s acceptable if it keeps the service up.

[16:17] Tom Becker: But from audit standpoint we need to know it happened.

[16:20] Jordan Lee: Yep, there’s an event and metrics.

[16:27] Derek Lin: Is it per-request or per-key? Like if candidate is overloaded, do you move an entire key group?

[16:33] Jordan Lee: In our current design it’s per-request at the last hop if there’s no healthy candidate backend. But again, it’s controlled.

[16:45] Priya Shah: Are you doing "shadow" stage? Like Stage 0 sends to candidate but doesn’t serve response.

[16:52] Mina Haddad: For Dedicated, we can do shadow if you have the capacity. But it’s not always feasible. In v1, Stage 0 is optional and more like internal validation.

[17:06] Ana Morales: Shadow is expensive.

[17:08] Mina Haddad: Exactly.

[17:11] Ethan Park: Let’s talk about how gate evaluation windows work. Gates define: metric query, aggregation (p95, rate), a threshold, a comparison operator, and an evaluation window (like 10 minutes). Evaluator runs on a cadence, e.g. every 60 seconds.

[17:32] Derek Lin: How do you avoid flapping? Like one bad minute triggers pause.

[17:36] Logan Wright: We can require consecutive failures, like 3 out of 5 intervals. Also we can use burn-rate style evaluation. But for v1, we’re keeping it simpler: windowed aggregates.

[17:52] Sean Gallagher: And if it pauses, it stays paused until manually resumed or rolled back, unless you set auto-resume (which we don’t recommend).

[18:03] Priya Shah: Good.

[18:06] Tom Becker: Permissions: who can approve? Is it only Redwood ops or can HelioBank do it.

[18:12] Ethan Park: Initially Redwood operators, with enterprise opt-in. The RBAC model supports tenant-scoped roles. So for you, it could be a HelioBank admin role that can approve/abort.

[18:30] Chloe Martin: But we’re gating that behind feature flag. We’ll coordinate.

[18:35] Priya Shah: Ok. Now, determinism again: if we route based on conversation_id, what about streaming requests? Do they all use same id?

[18:44] Jordan Lee: Streaming uses a single request context for the stream. If your app uses multiple calls per conversation, it should reuse the conversation_id. Then you get consistent canary exposure.

[19:01] Ana Morales: If we don’t pass the key on some calls, could a conversation split.

[19:05] Jordan Lee: Yes. We’ll document it, and the SDK can help.

[19:12] Derek Lin: Another edge: retries. If a request retries, does it hit same backend.

[19:18] Jordan Lee: Same candidate/baseline decision if same key. Backend selection may change depending on health.

[19:28] Mina Haddad: Typically that’s what you want. If one replica is unhealthy, you don’t want to stick.

[19:33] Priya Shah: On missing metrics, we’ve had incidents where metrics pipeline lags but service is fine. If rollout pauses for that, it could slow releases but ok.

[19:46] Sean Gallagher: That’s the tradeoff. For Dedicated, safety > speed.

[19:52] Logan Wright: We’re also adding evaluator health dashboards so you can distinguish "paused due to real regression" vs "paused due to metrics missing".

[20:06] Chloe Martin: In the stage detail view, there’ll be a badge like “Paused: Missing metrics (queue_depth)” vs “Paused: p95 latency threshold exceeded”.

[20:18] Tom Becker: Nice.

[20:20] Ethan Park: Let’s walk through a concrete example. Stage 1 is 5% for 15 minutes. Gates: p95 latency < 800ms, 5xx < 0.2%, queue depth < 20, metric freshness < 3m, and min requests > 5k.

[20:41] Priya Shah: 5k requests at 5% means we need 100k total in window. That’s high.

[20:47] Sean Gallagher: Right, we’ll tune per tenant. That’s why defaults are recommendations.

[20:53] Ana Morales: For our critical routes we can meet that, but not all.

[20:58] Ethan Park: Exactly. It can be per-route eventually. For v1, it’s per-pool but can have route filters.

[21:10] Derek Lin: Wait, per-pool but route filters? That’s important.

[21:14] Ethan Park: You can scope a rollout plan to a subset of routes on that pool, so you don’t have to roll everything.

[21:22] Priya Shah: That’s what we need. We have multiple apps on same pool.

[21:27] Mina Haddad: For Dedicated, we still maintain isolation at route level in routing, so that’s feasible.

[21:36] Speaker 1: Sorry, was that “root” or “route”? The transcript will probably get that wrong.

[21:39] Chloe Martin: Route. (laughs)

[21:41] Ethan Park: Yep route.

[21:45] Tom Becker: Audit logs for route-scoped changes should include route ids.

[21:49] Ethan Park: They will.

[21:52] Derek Lin: Another failure mode: what if routing and evaluator disagree on what stage is active. Like stale snapshots.

[22:01] Ethan Park: Evaluator uses control plane as source of truth. Routing uses snapshots. If routing is stale, it might keep an older stage weight temporarily. That’s why we show “applied” status and alert if drift is too long.

[22:17] Sean Gallagher: We also treat prolonged drift as incident-worthy, because it means the rollout isn’t doing what you think.

[22:24] Priya Shah: Ok. How do you detect drift?

[22:27] Mina Haddad: Routing reports the plan_version it is enforcing via metrics. Evaluator/control plane knows desired plan_version. We compare.

[22:40] Logan Wright: Exactly. Low cardinality, per pool.

[22:45] Ana Morales: On capacity guardrails, can you explain headroom rule.

[22:49] Mina Haddad: We set a minimum headroom percentage. Like if current utilization is above 85% sustained, you can’t promote. Also, if queue depth is rising, you can’t promote. And we can integrate with autoscaling if you have burst nodes, but for reserved pools it’s limited.

[23:12] Derek Lin: So you might block stage advancement even if gates pass, if headroom not enough.

[23:18] Mina Haddad: Yes. Think of it as a meta-gate.

[23:23] Priya Shah: That’s good. We got burned by "canary" that actually created more load due to duplication.

[23:29] Jordan Lee: Another nuance: candidate may have different token throughput. Even if traffic share is 25%, token volume might not be 25%. We measure by tokens too.

[23:43] Logan Wright: Yep, we have token-level metrics for throughput and latency; gates can be per request or per token.

[23:52] Ana Morales: Per token would be more accurate.

[23:55] Logan Wright: Agreed, but it’s sometimes harder to reason about. We can do both.

[24:01] Tom Becker: Does any of this involve storing prompts? We can’t.

[24:05] Ethan Park: No, gates are based on aggregated metrics, not content. Quality signals are optional and usually run on your eval set, not production prompts.

[24:17] Priya Shah: Ok.

[24:19] Derek Lin: You mentioned optional quality signals. How does that work.

[24:23] Ethan Park: For some customers we can run periodic evals and treat regression as a gate, but not in v1 for all routes.

[24:33] Ana Morales: Fine.

[24:36] Chloe Martin: If it helps, in Console the gate list is extensible. So later you can add “eval score >= X”.

[24:44] Priya Shah: Cool.

[24:46] Ethan Park: I want to cover idempotency and retries for approvals. Approvals are events with unique ids. If an approver clicks twice, it’s one approval.

[25:00] Tom Becker: And approval identity comes from SSO?

[25:03] Chloe Martin: If enabled, yes. Otherwise Redwood operator identity.

[25:08] Priya Shah: On SSO, we’re SAML.

[25:10] Chloe Martin: Supported.

[25:12] Derek Lin: Let’s talk about what happens when a stage is promoted. Does routing instantly send 25%? Or does it ramp.

[25:20] Jordan Lee: For v1, it’s a step function at promotion time. But we can optionally do a ramp over a few minutes. Not sure if we’ll ship that first.

[25:31] Sean Gallagher: Step is simpler and more deterministic. Ramp introduces more states.

[25:37] Priya Shah: We can handle step, as long as it’s auditable.

[25:41] Ana Morales: Step at 25% might be scary.

[25:44] Mina Haddad: That’s why you have stages. 5 -> 10 -> 25, etc.

[25:50] Derek Lin: Ok.

[25:52] Ethan Park: Any other determinism concerns?

[25:55] Priya Shah: One more: we sometimes do per-region pools. If we do the same rollout plan in two regions, do the same users hit different stage because of different hashing.

[26:05] Jordan Lee: The hashing function is the same. But if user traffic is split by region, you can’t guarantee the same user is in the same bucket across regions unless you share the same key and the same stage weight. If the weights match, the decision matches.

[26:22] Priya Shah: Good.

[26:24] Derek Lin: Let’s shift to monitoring. How do we know gate evaluator is healthy.

[26:30] Logan Wright: We have metrics: evaluator tick duration, last successful evaluation time per pool, percent of evaluations with missing metrics, and so on. There will be dashboards.

[26:45] Sean Gallagher: And alerts: if evaluator lag > X, or if rollouts stuck in WAITING_APPROVAL too long, etc.

[26:56] Priya Shah: Nice.

[26:58] Ana Morales: Stuck waiting approval is not an alert for us (laughs). But stuck in “promoting” might be.

[27:05] Chloe Martin: Yep, we differentiate.

[27:09] Ethan Park: We’re at time check—about halfway. I’ll pause. What do you need to decide to move forward with beta.

[27:18] Priya Shah: We need: 1) exact semantics of routing key and what SDK support looks like, 2) what gates are required, and 3) what happens on failure—hold vs rollback policies.

[27:33] Derek Lin: Also evidence for change management. Audit logs and export.

[27:37] Tom Becker: Yes.

[27:39] Ethan Park: Great. We can provide those.

[27:42] Mina Haddad: We’ll send a routing determinism one-pager.

[27:45] Logan Wright: And I’ll confirm metrics freshness SLA.

[27:48] Sean Gallagher: And we’ll send recommended defaults for Dedicated.

[27:55] Priya Shah: Awesome.

[28:00] (crosstalk)

[28:03] Ethan Park: Let’s do a quick scenario: if candidate increases latency, gate triggers hold, and you choose rollback. What does rollback do? It sets weight back to 0 candidate (or previous stage) and marks rollout as aborted.

[28:21] Derek Lin: But does it also revert the underlying deployment? Like uninstall candidate.

[28:26] Mina Haddad: Not automatically. It stops sending traffic, but the candidate artifacts may still be present on the nodes. That makes subsequent attempts faster.

[28:38] Derek Lin: For compliance, that’s okay.

[28:41] Priya Shah: But it could still consume memory.

[28:44] Mina Haddad: True. There’s a cleanup step. In v1, manual. Later, automatic garbage collection.

[28:53] Ana Morales: Ok.

[28:55] Tom Becker: Is there any case where rollback fails and we’re stuck.

[29:00] Ethan Park: Control-plane write can fail, but then nothing changes; routing stays at old state. We treat that as incident. We also have a break-glass operator override.

[29:13] Sean Gallagher: And we can force traffic to baseline at routing layer as emergency.

[29:19] Priya Shah: That’s important.

[29:22] Derek Lin: Another question: are you doing gradual node-level rollout or request-level.

[29:28] Mina Haddad: For Dedicated, it’s request-level traffic split enforced by routing. Under the hood, candidate and baseline can be deployed on subsets of nodes depending on capacity, but you interact with it as traffic weights.

[29:45] Ana Morales: So canary could be running on fewer GPUs.

[29:48] Mina Haddad: Yes. That’s part of the capacity guardrail.

[29:52] Jordan Lee: Determinism is about the request assignment, not pinning to a specific GPU.

[30:00] Priya Shah: ok.

[30:02] Chloe Martin: I’ll mention one UI thing: stage detail shows both gate status and capacity warnings, like “candidate replicas at max concurrency”.

[30:14] Derek Lin: Nice.

[30:16] Ethan Park: Any other concerns?

[30:18] Ana Morales: Minor: if we have multiple models on pool, can we stage rollouts per model.

[30:25] Ethan Park: Plan can reference a “target” which includes model version and runtime config. If multiple, you create separate rollouts scoped to routes.
